questions.question: What is sustainable development?
questions.modelAnswer: Meeting the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
markingPoints: Meeting the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

questions.question: Define a finite resource.
questions.modelAnswer: Used faster than it is formed.
markingPoints: Used faster than it is formed.

questions.question: Define a renewable resource.
questions.modelAnswer: Replenished on a human timescale.
markingPoints: Replenished on a human timescale.

questions.question: Define a sustainable resource.
questions.modelAnswer: Meets present needs without compromising future needs.
markingPoints: Meets present needs without compromising future needs.

questions.question: Explain why renewable does not always mean impact-free.
questions.modelAnswer: Extraction, land use and energy use can still harm ecosystems; use must not exceed replacement.
markingPoints: Extraction, land use and energy use can still harm ecosystems; use must not exceed replacement.

questions.question: Define potable water.
questions.modelAnswer: Water that is safe to drink; it does not need to be pure water.
markingPoints: Water that is safe to drink; it does not need to be pure water.

questions.question: Why is most potable water in the UK obtained from fresh water rather than seawater?
questions.modelAnswer: Fresh water needs less treatment and far less energy than desalination, so it is usually cheaper.
markingPoints: Fresh water needs less treatment and far less energy than desalination, so it is usually cheaper.

questions.question: State the main stages used to produce potable water from fresh water.
questions.modelAnswer:
Choose a suitable source.
Pass through filter beds to remove solids.
Sterilise using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
markingPoints: Choose a suitable source.
Pass through filter beds to remove solids.
Sterilise using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

questions.question: Explain why filtration alone cannot remove dissolved salts from water.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dissolved ions/particles are much smaller than filter-paper pores and pass through with water.
Distillation or another desalination method is required.
markingPoints: Dissolved ions/particles are much smaller than filter-paper pores and pass through with water.
Distillation or another desalination method is required.

questions.question: Describe the laboratory production of potable water from a sample containing insoluble solids and dissolved salts.
questions.modelAnswer:
Filter to remove insoluble solids.
Distil by boiling and condensing water to separate dissolved salts.
Collect distillate.
Test pH or dissolved solids as appropriate.
Potable means safe to drink, not chemically pure.
markingPoints: Filter to remove insoluble solids.
Distil by boiling and condensing water to separate dissolved salts.
Collect distillate.
Test pH or dissolved solids as appropriate.
Potable means safe to drink, not chemically pure.

questions.question: Explain why potable water is not necessarily pure water.
questions.modelAnswer: It can contain safe levels of dissolved minerals.
markingPoints: It can contain safe levels of dissolved minerals.

questions.question: Describe two stages in treating freshwater to make potable water.
questions.modelAnswer:
Filter/sediment to remove solids
Sterilise by chlorine, ozone or UV to kill microbes.
markingPoints: Filter/sediment to remove solids
Sterilise by chlorine, ozone or UV to kill microbes.

questions.question: A dish is 42.36 g empty and 42.61 g after evaporating 50.0 cm3 water. Calculate dissolved-solids concentration in g/dm3.
questions.modelAnswer:
Solids=0.25 g.
Volume=0.0500 dm3.
Concentration=0.25/0.0500=5.0 g/dm3.
markingPoints: Solids=0.25 g.
Volume=0.0500 dm3.
Concentration=0.25/0.0500=5.0 g/dm3.

questions.question: Compare distillation and reverse osmosis for desalination, including mechanism, energy/cost and environmental issue.
questions.modelAnswer:
Distillation evaporates/condenses.
High heat energy.
RO high pressure through membrane.
Electrical energy/membrane.
Both costly.
Concentrated brine/ecosystem and carbon impacts.
Suitability depends on energy/water scarcity.
markingPoints: Distillation evaporates/condenses.
High heat energy.
RO high pressure through membrane.
Electrical energy/membrane.
Both costly.
Concentrated brine/ecosystem and carbon impacts.
Suitability depends on energy/water scarcity.

questions.question: Compare producing potable water from fresh water and seawater.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fresh water: choose source, filter and sterilise.
Generally lower energy/cost but supply may be limited/contaminated.
Seawater desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis supplies arid areas but uses much energy, costs more and creates concentrated brine impacts.
markingPoints: Fresh water: choose source, filter and sterilise.
Generally lower energy/cost but supply may be limited/contaminated.
Seawater desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis supplies arid areas but uses much energy, costs more and creates concentrated brine impacts.

questions.question: Plan how to compare the dissolved-solid content of two water samples by evaporation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dry and weigh identical evaporating basins.
Add equal accurately measured water volumes.
Evaporate safely to dryness.
Cool and reweigh.
Calculate residue mass per unit volume.
Repeat.
Control basin and heating method.
Avoid spitting and contamination.
markingPoints: Dry and weigh identical evaporating basins.
Add equal accurately measured water volumes.
Evaporate safely to dryness.
Cool and reweigh.
Calculate residue mass per unit volume.
Repeat.
Control basin and heating method.
Avoid spitting and contamination.

questions.question: Plan the required practical to compare samples of water by measuring pH, dissolved solids and purity after distillation. Include one safety precaution.
questions.modelAnswer:
Measure pH consistently.
Evaporate known volume in preweighed dish, dry/cool/reweigh for solids.
Distil with anti-bumping, condenser water flow, collect distillate.
Eye protection/heat care.
Repeats, same volumes, avoid contamination.
markingPoints: Measure pH consistently.
Evaporate known volume in preweighed dish, dry/cool/reweigh for solids.
Distil with anti-bumping, condenser water flow, collect distillate.
Eye protection/heat care.
Repeats, same volumes, avoid contamination.

questions.question: What happens during aerobic biological treatment of sewage effluent?
questions.modelAnswer: Aerobic microorganisms break down/digest organic matter in the presence of oxygen.
markingPoints: Aerobic microorganisms break down/digest organic matter in the presence of oxygen.

questions.question: What happens to sewage sludge during anaerobic digestion?
questions.modelAnswer: Anaerobic microorganisms digest it without oxygen, producing biogas and treated sludge.
markingPoints: Anaerobic microorganisms digest it without oxygen, producing biogas and treated sludge.

questions.question: What is the purpose of screening and grit removal during sewage treatment?
questions.modelAnswer: To remove large objects and solid grit before later treatment stages.
markingPoints: To remove large objects and solid grit before later treatment stages.

questions.question: State the four main stages of sewage treatment.
questions.modelAnswer: Screening and grit removal; sedimentation; anaerobic digestion of sludge; aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
markingPoints: Screening and grit removal; sedimentation; anaerobic digestion of sludge; aerobic biological treatment of effluent.

questions.question: Describe sewage treatment from screening to discharge, including sludge and effluent pathways.
questions.modelAnswer:
Screen grit/large objects.
Sedimentation separates sludge/effluent.
Anaerobic digestion of sludge produces biogas.
Aerobic microbes treat effluent/organic matter.
Discharge after treatment.
Industrial toxins may need removal.
markingPoints: Screen grit/large objects.
Sedimentation separates sludge/effluent.
Anaerobic digestion of sludge produces biogas.
Aerobic microbes treat effluent/organic matter.
Discharge after treatment.
Industrial toxins may need removal.

questions.question: What is a low-grade ore?
questions.modelAnswer: An ore containing a small percentage/concentration of the desired metal compound.
markingPoints: An ore containing a small percentage/concentration of the desired metal compound.

questions.question: How does bioleaching extract metals from low-grade ores?
questions.modelAnswer: Bacteria convert metal compounds into soluble metal ions, producing a leachate from which the metal can be recovered.
markingPoints: Bacteria convert metal compounds into soluble metal ions, producing a leachate from which the metal can be recovered.

questions.question: How does phytomining produce a metal-rich material?
questions.modelAnswer:
Plants absorb metal ions from soil.
Plants are harvested and burned.
The ash contains a higher concentration of metal compounds.
markingPoints: Plants absorb metal ions from soil.
Plants are harvested and burned.
The ash contains a higher concentration of metal compounds.

questions.question: Compare phytomining and bioleaching for low-grade copper ores and state how copper can be recovered from the resulting material.
questions.modelAnswer:
Plants absorb ions then harvested/burned, metal from ash.
Bacteria produce leachate.
Lower-grade/less landscape damage and energy than conventional mining but slow/land/process issues.
Recover by displacement with iron or electrolysis.
Purity differs.
markingPoints: Plants absorb ions then harvested/burned, metal from ash.
Bacteria produce leachate.
Lower-grade/less landscape damage and energy than conventional mining but slow/land/process issues.
Recover by displacement with iron or electrolysis.
Purity differs.

questions.question: Why can life-cycle assessments contain subjective judgements?
questions.modelAnswer: Environmental impacts may be difficult to quantify and different analysts may choose different boundaries or weight impacts differently.
markingPoints: Environmental impacts may be difficult to quantify and different analysts may choose different boundaries or weight impacts differently.

questions.question: Name the four stages considered in a life-cycle assessment.
questions.modelAnswer: Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use; disposal at the end of life.
markingPoints: Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use; disposal at the end of life.

questions.question: State the four stages considered in a life-cycle assessment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Raw-material extraction and processing.
Manufacture/packaging.
Use.
End-of-life disposal, reuse or recycling.
markingPoints: Raw-material extraction and processing.
Manufacture/packaging.
Use.
End-of-life disposal, reuse or recycling.

questions.question: Explain why two LCAs of the same product may give different results.
questions.modelAnswer: They can use different boundaries, data, assumptions and weighting of impacts.
markingPoints: They can use different boundaries, data, assumptions and weighting of impacts.

questions.question: Name the four main stages of a life-cycle assessment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Raw-material extraction 
Manufacture and packaging
Use
Disposal/end of life.
markingPoints: Raw-material extraction
Manufacture and packaging
Use
Disposal/end of life.

questions.question: Evaluate replacing a metal car panel with a carbon-fibre composite using a life-cycle approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
Compare raw materials, manufacture energy/emissions, mass/fuel savings during use, durability/repair, transport, recyclability/end of life and cost.
Lighter use phase may offset high manufacture.
Conclusion depends on lifetime, energy mix and reuse/recycling data.
markingPoints: Compare raw materials, manufacture energy/emissions, mass/fuel savings during use, durability/repair, transport, recyclability/end of life and cost.
Lighter use phase may offset high manufacture.
Conclusion depends on lifetime, energy mix and reuse/recycling data.

questions.question: Evaluate paper bags using a life-cycle assessment.
questions.modelAnswer: Consider raw materials, manufacturing, transport, use and disposal. Paper is renewable and biodegradable, but production can use water and energy and bags may be heavier to transport.
markingPoints: Consider raw materials, manufacturing, transport, use and disposal. Paper is renewable and biodegradable, but production can use water and energy and bags may be heavier to transport.

questions.question: Evaluate reusable plastic bags using a life-cycle assessment.
questions.modelAnswer: Consider raw materials, manufacturing, transport, use and disposal. They can be reused many times, reducing waste per use, but are made from non-renewable resources and may persist if discarded.
markingPoints: Consider raw materials, manufacturing, transport, use and disposal. They can be reused many times, reducing waste per use, but are made from non-renewable resources and may persist if discarded.

questions.question: Explain why a life-cycle assessment conclusion depends on system boundaries and weighting.
questions.modelAnswer:
Including or excluding extraction, manufacture, transport, use and disposal changes totals.
Different impacts use different units and value judgements are needed to weight carbon, water, toxicity and waste, so assumptions must be stated and sensitivity considered.
markingPoints: Including or excluding extraction, manufacture, transport, use and disposal changes totals.
Different impacts use different units and value judgements are needed to weight carbon, water, toxicity and waste, so assumptions must be stated and sensitivity considered.

questions.question: Why does recycling metals usually save energy compared with extracting metals from ores?
questions.modelAnswer:
Extraction and processing ores require mining and energy-intensive chemical processes.
Recycling avoids much of this.
markingPoints: Extraction and processing ores require mining and energy-intensive chemical processes.
Recycling avoids much of this.

questions.question: Explain why recycling metals can reduce environmental impact but is not impact-free.
questions.modelAnswer:
It reduces mining, finite-resource use, waste and often energy demand/emissions.
However collection, transport, sorting, cleaning and remelting use energy.
Contamination can reduce quality, and some material is lost.
markingPoints: It reduces mining, finite-resource use, waste and often energy demand/emissions.
However collection, transport, sorting, cleaning and remelting use energy.
Contamination can reduce quality, and some material is lost.

questions.question: Compare reducing, reusing and recycling aluminium cans using energy, raw materials, transport and material quality.
questions.modelAnswer:
Reduce avoids production.
Reuse avoids remelting but cleaning/transport/design.
Recycle saves ore and usually energy but collection/sorting/remelting needed.
Aluminium recyclable with little quality loss.
markingPoints: Reduce avoids production.
Reuse avoids remelting but cleaning/transport/design.
Recycle saves ore and usually energy but collection/sorting/remelting needed.
Aluminium recyclable with little quality loss.

questions.question: Evaluate whether recycled aluminium is always environmentally preferable to newly extracted aluminium.
questions.modelAnswer:
Recycling usually saves energy and ore and reduces landfill, but collection, sorting, transport and contamination use resources.
The conclusion depends on transport distances, energy source, recovery rate and product quality.
Compare quantified life-cycle data.
markingPoints: Recycling usually saves energy and ore and reduces landfill, but collection, sorting, transport and contamination use resources.
The conclusion depends on transport distances, energy source, recovery rate and product quality.
Compare quantified life-cycle data.

questions.modelAnswer:
Use cleaned identical iron nails in sealed tubes: dry air with a drying agent, boiled water with oil to exclude oxygen, and water plus air.
Keep time and temperature constant.
Compare rust.
Include repeats.
Rust requires both oxygen and water.
markingPoints: Use cleaned identical iron nails in sealed tubes: dry air with a drying agent, boiled water with oil to exclude oxygen, and water plus air.
Keep time and temperature constant.
Compare rust.
Include repeats.
Rust requires both oxygen and water.

questions.question: State the two conditions required for iron to rust.
questions.modelAnswer: Both oxygen and water must be present.
markingPoints: Both oxygen and water must be present.

questions.question: How does galvanising protect iron?
questions.modelAnswer:
A zinc coating forms a barrier.
If scratched, the more reactive zinc oxidises preferentially and provides sacrificial protection.
markingPoints: A zinc coating forms a barrier.
If scratched, the more reactive zinc oxidises preferentially and provides sacrificial protection.

questions.question: Explain sacrificial protection of iron using zinc, including electron transfer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Zinc is more reactive and oxidises preferentially: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Electrons supplied to iron prevent iron atoms oxidising, so iron does not rust even if coating is scratched, while zinc is consumed.
markingPoints: Zinc is more reactive and oxidises preferentially: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Electrons supplied to iron prevent iron atoms oxidising, so iron does not rust even if coating is scratched, while zinc is consumed.

questions.question: Explain rusting requirements and evaluate painting, galvanising and sacrificial protection when a coating is scratched.
questions.modelAnswer:
Rust needs O2+water.
Paint barrier fails at scratch.
Galvanising zinc barrier and zinc oxidises preferentially if scratched.
Sacrificial metal must be more reactive and replaced.
Choose for environment/cost.
markingPoints: Rust needs O2+water.
Paint barrier fails at scratch.
Galvanising zinc barrier and zinc oxidises preferentially if scratched.
Sacrificial metal must be more reactive and replaced.
Choose for environment/cost.

questions.question: Compare a ceramic, a polymer and a composite for a bicycle component.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ceramic is hard/heat resistant but brittle.
Polymer is light, corrosion-resistant and formable but may soften/creep.
Composite combines reinforcement and matrix for high strength-to-mass but may cost more and be difficult to recycle.
Choice must match component forces and conditions.
markingPoints: Ceramic is hard/heat resistant but brittle.
Polymer is light, corrosion-resistant and formable but may soften/creep.
Composite combines reinforcement and matrix for high strength-to-mass but may cost more and be difficult to recycle.
Choice must match component forces and conditions.

questions.question: Explain why alloys are often harder than pure metals and select between ceramic, polymer and composite for a bicycle component.
questions.modelAnswer:
Different-sized alloy atoms distort layers and stop sliding.
Selection must use stated property: ceramic hard/heat-resistant but brittle.
Polymer light/flexible but may soften.
Composite high strength-to-mass/designable but costly/recycling difficult.
markingPoints: Different-sized alloy atoms distort layers and stop sliding.
Selection must use stated property: ceramic hard/heat-resistant but brittle.
Polymer light/flexible but may soften.
Composite high strength-to-mass/designable but costly/recycling difficult.

questions.question: Why are composites useful engineering materials?
questions.modelAnswer: They combine a matrix/binder with a reinforcement, giving useful properties from both, such as high strength with low mass.
markingPoints: They combine a matrix/binder with a reinforcement, giving useful properties from both, such as high strength with low mass.

questions.question: Explain how ammonia is used to make ammonium nitrate fertiliser.
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonia reacts with nitric acid to form ammonium nitrate.
markingPoints: Ammonia reacts with nitric acid to form ammonium nitrate.

questions.question: Explain why NPK fertilisers are formulations.
questions.modelAnswer: They contain measured proportions of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds for plant needs.
markingPoints: They contain measured proportions of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds for plant needs.
